# Why Asklēpiós is spelled that way — and what it costs to get it right

There is a version of this name the early internet had to settle for: *asklepios*. This is the file on how **Asklēpiós** replaced it.

Born from catastrophe — cut from the womb of the dying Korōnis by his father Apóllōn — Asklēpiós was raised by the centaur Cheirōn, who taught him the pharmaka of roots and the surgery of the knife.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Asklēpiós
- **ASCII form:** asklepios
- **Meaning:** "Uncertain; possibly related to ἀσκαλαβώτης (lizard) or a pre-Greek healing root"
- **Domain of influence:** Medicine, Healing, Renewal
- **Pantheon:** Greek
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Original script:** Ἀσκληπιός
- **Series:** The Restoration Files, No. 39 of 282

## The Name Before the Marks

The name is attested as **Ἀσκληπιός**, as LSJ and Homeric Hymns preserve it. On the evidence, it means "Uncertain; possibly related to ἀσκαλαβώτης (lizard) or a pre-Greek healing root".

Strip **Asklēpiós** to *asklepios* and 2 pieces of evidence vanish:

- **e → ē** — Macron marks the long vowel: the vowel length the ASCII form cannot show.
- **o → ó** — Stress mark (acute/tone): the stress position the ASCII form cannot show.

None of these marks is decoration. Each one is a fact about how the name was spoken, and each one is checkable against the scholarly record the temple cites.

Spoken, the name runs `/a.skliː.pi.ós/` — ah-SKLAY-pee-OSS, with the stress on the ultima and a long ē.

## The Temple That Stands Now

The restored name is not a plaque; it is an address. The temple of **Asklēpiós** lives at [/sites/asklepios/](/sites/asklepios/), with its mythology in the [lore halls](/sites/asklepios/lore/), its peer-reviewed record in the [Scholarly Edition](/sites/asklepios/scholars/), and its place in the pattern atlas on the [patterns floor](/sites/asklepios/patterns/).

What survives here cannot be shown in ASCII: a feature of the original that the fallback alphabet flattens. That is the Tier-1 test, and this name passes it without argument.

## Where the Name Stood First

The sanctuary at Epidaurus — a UNESCO World Heritage site — preserves the abaton, the circular tholos (possibly the god's labyrinthine "dance floor" designed by Polykleitos), and the theatre where healed patients watched drama as therapy. The iamata stelai (IG IV².1 121–124), the surviving late-4th-century-BCE originals, list some seventy cures. At Kos, the terraced Asklepieion adjoins the Hippocratic plane tree's descendants; at Rome the Tiber Island temple's travertine snake-prow survives. The temple on the web is the newest of these addresses — the first one that fits in a pocket.

## The Archetype at Work

The [pattern atlas](/patterns/) seats this temple in **3 industries**, each match argued and weighted: **Biotech, Longevity & Life Sciences** (he healed so well that Zeús destroyed him for emptying the underworld — the physician who pressed the boundary of death itself.); **Healthcare, Pharma & Medicine** (the surgeon-son of Apóllōn whose sanctuaries were antiquity’s hospitals; his snake-entwined staff still hangs over every pharmacy.); **Yoga, Meditation & Holistic Wellness** (incubation sanctuaries were antiquity’s wellness retreats — sleep, dream, cure.). The [Resonance File](/sites/asklepios/blog/resonance/) reads those seats through the myths themselves.

The [Sacred Texts collection](/texts/) holds [Theogony](/texts/theogony/), [Homeric Hymns](/texts/homeric-hymns/), and [Works and Days](/texts/works-and-days/) — the primary sources the temple's scholarship is built on. The temple is the argument; the texts are the evidence.
